blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Identify the causes of market failure - public goods, merit and demerit goods, external costs, external benefits, the abuse of monopoly power, and factor immobility - and analyse how each leaves the market at the wrong level of output.

blocks.heading: Six causes, one thread
blocks.text: The causes share one thread: some cost or benefit never reaches the price. Public goods fail because non-payers cannot be excluded. Merit goods are under-consumed because consumers undervalue them; demerit goods over-consumed because consumers undercount their harm. Goods with external costs are over-produced because the damage to others stays outside the price; goods with external benefits are under-produced because the gains to others never raise demand. A dominant seller may hold output back to keep prices up. Immobile workers and capital cannot reach the uses that need them.

blocks.heading: A cost imposed on others
blocks.text: Otavi Charcoal Works earns N$40 000 a season burning wood waste. Its smoke drifts over 60 homesteads, and each spends N$250 a season on cleaning and clinic visits, so the season carries 60 x N$250 = N$15 000 of costs the firm never pays. Because the price of charcoal holds none of this, the market reads the activity as more profitable than it is for society, and output tends to sit above the level society would choose. A paper mill on a river in Vietnam works the same way: the fishers downstream pay, the price does not.

blocks.heading: The free-rider chain
blocks.text: Start with flood defences at Walvis Bay. Because each protected street stays dry whether or not its households contributed, each household is likely to wait for others to pay. This waiting is the free-rider problem, and it causes private providers to withdraw. The consequence is under-provision relative to what the defences are worth to the town as a whole - the classic shortfall of a public good, landing on the households and firms the waters would reach.

blocks.heading: Trapped factors and dominant sellers
blocks.text: Factor immobility fails markets in a second way. When net-mending work at Walvis Bay declines, the workers cannot at once become plumbers in Windhoek: their skills are fixed to the old trade, and homes and family keep them where they are. Labour then sits unused in one place while needs go unmet in another. And where a single dominant seller stands behind barriers to entry, it may hold output below the level a market of many small sellers would produce, to keep its price up.

blocks.heading: Abuse of monopoly power
blocks.text: Monopoly power is the power of a single seller, or of one seller far larger than any rival, to set its price because buyers have few other places to go. It rests on barriers to entry that keep rivals out, such as high start-up costs, distance from other suppliers, or control of a key resource. Holding that power is not in itself a market failure; abusing it is. A seller abuses its power when it raises its price above the level rivals would allow, holds back output, lets quality or service slip, or blocks newcomers. Take Karas Cement Works, the single cement producer within reach of builders in southern Namibia. Suppose it raises its price from N$95 to N$120 a bag and monthly sales fall from 10 000 to 8 000 bags. Its revenue rises by just N$10 000, from N$950 000 to N$960 000, and with less cement to make its costs are likely to fall, so its profit rises. Builders pay N$25 more a bag, and 2 000 fewer bags a month go into houses, shops and clinics. Fewer resources go into building than society wants: that is the misallocation.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The demand and supply curves of topics 2.3 and 2.4 meet at the equilibrium this topic questions; the market price they set is the one that leaves these causes unpaid.
